about: The words of the chain saga_rhine_frisia, THE LAW THAT WAS ONLY SAID (Data/encounters/chain_saga_rhine_frisia_793.json; Design/content/chains/saga_rhine_frisia.md): how the law of the Frisians came to the emperor's pen in 802. Every title, intention, line and label key of its fourteen cards; an outcome text for every option (keys '...out_<option>', named in each option's note: the engine shows the effects' own facts, the outcome texts are for the integrator); the four news items the finales post; and one 'art.<card id>' line for each card's picture. People named in the words: Wlemar and Saxmund (real: the two wise men of the Lex Frisionum's additions; everything about them but their names and their judgements is invented), Bernlef the singer (real), Boniface and Saint Martin, King Charles, the emperor, and his son. Nothing is quoted from any translation: what the wise men say of the law follows the Lex Frisionum (tit. I, XIV, XVIII; Additio I, II, VI, XI) in our own plain words, and the son's news of 814 follows the Astronomer's Life of Louis c. 24 in ours. 'Shilling' is the law's solidus, a count of two, two and a half or three pennies by land. Nobody says 'Lex'. Written 6 Oct 2026; a draft for the user to overwrite.

entries.text: Seven named
A man was knifed in the press at yesterday's wool sale and nobody saw the hand. His brother has named the seven who stood nearest. Your steersman is the fifth.
Seven named, and no more than seven: that is the law. Each swears with eleven of his own rank. Then the lots go on the altar, because eleven friends prove a man is liked, not that he is clean.
Two twigs, wrapped in clean wool. One is cut with a cross. If the cross is lifted, all seven go home. If the bare one, each man cuts his own mark, and we draw until one twig is left.
The law says a priest draws, or a boy without guilt. I would rather the boy. A boy has no opinion of anyone yet.
I sold a fleece and scratched my ear. That is all I did in that crowd. I have eight who will swear. I need eleven.
A shipmaster's oath is good here if he is a free Frisian. Nobody will ask where his boat was built.

You go east of the Lauwers? Then carry a word to Saxmund at the Ems mouth. Say: the three lands should agree what a man is worth before a stranger asks. Say it as I said it. It is not a thing to write.
Swear with him, and find the other helpers
Pay the brother to drop the fifth name
Let the law run and get the wool aboard

You swear on the relics with ten others, and two of them you talked into it yourself. The boy lifts a twig out of the wool, and it is the one with the cross. Seven men go home. Wlemar tells the dead man's brother he must now think again, and that this is what law is for.

The boy lifts the bare twig. Seven men cut seven marks, and it takes three days and a good deal of your ale before the last twig left on the altar is a cattle dealer's from Aalsum. Your steersman's came out fourth. The dealer pays. He does not deny it for long.

The brother takes thirty pennies and finds he is no longer sure about the fifth man. Six swear, and the lot is drawn for six. Wlemar says it is allowed. He says it the way a man says a fish is fresh enough.

You load fleeces while your steersman goes round the houses asking men to swear for him. He has his eleven by dark, and the lot clears him. He does not speak of it again. He does not sing at the oar for a week either.
Beyond the Lauwers
Saxmund, who says the law for the land between the Lauwers and the Weser, is mending a net outside his sister's house. He hears Wlemar's word through to the end before he puts the needle down.
Before a stranger asks. He means the king's clerks. Wlemar smells weather a year off. It is his one fault.
What is a man worth? Here, a noble is a hundred and six shillings and two pennies, which sounds more than over the water. We count two pennies to the shilling. Do not envy us.

Ask him what a dead man's land is worth. My husband went to the Weser in the year the churches burned and did not come back. For that, King Charles took from all who rose the right to leave land to their sons. Mine plough their father's field for the count's man.
It was done by law. That is the worst that can be said of a law.
Bernlef says the old judgements go best to a tune. A man forgets a number. He does not forget where the verse turns.
If you want to be useful and not only sorry: four black quernstones from the Rhine. Ours are worn as thin as plates.
Take Saxmund west to Winaldum in your boat
Take the widow's order for quernstones
You have said the word; go on with your trade

Saxmund comes aboard with a net, a cheese and no farewell worth the name. He sits in the bow and watches how your men handle the flats, and says once that the channel was further north in his father's day. He means it kindly.

The widow cuts the order on a stick and splits it, half for her and half for you: four stones, before the winter after this one, and she will pay over the price. Saxmund says he will go west by his cousin's boat when the hay is in.
You have said it as it was said to you. Saxmund nods and takes up the net again. He will go west when the hay is in, he says, and not before. Wlemar can wait. He is good at it.
Three numbers for one man
On the terp at Winaldum two wise men sit with a heap of beans between them, pricing a dead noble in three lands. They want a man who handles the king's new pennies every day.

Here a noble is eighty shillings, at three pennies the shilling. Beyond the Lauwers a hundred and six and two pennies, at two. West of the Vlie a hundred, at two and a half. Three numbers for one man.
It may be one number said three ways. Or it may be that you are cheap.
And all of it was judged in the old light pennies. The king's new ones are heavier, since the hungry year. You take them over the gunwale every day. Reckon it.
He reckons the tide well enough. I have seen him do it.
The west has not come. The old man at Medemelacha says his legs are finished with boats. Somebody must fetch what he knows before he takes it under the turf.
Reckon the three scales in the king's new pennies
Reckon it so the middle land comes out dearest
Say a carrier is no reckoner

Eighty threes are two hundred and forty. A hundred and six twos and two more are two hundred and fourteen. A hundred at two and a half are two hundred and fifty. You say so, and that the new penny is heavier by about a third, so nobody's dead are as dear as they sound. Saxmund counts the beans again and finds no fault. Wlemar pays you with a riddle about counting, which is what he has.
You lose the count at the half pennies. Wlemar finishes it on his fingers while you are still moving beans, and is kind about it, which is worse.

You let the middle land's shilling stand a little fat. A Westergo farmer who has been listening sends twenty pennies down to your boat that evening. Saxmund counts the beans himself afterwards and says nothing to you at all.
Wlemar nods. A man who knows what he is not, he says, is half a wise man. They go back to the beans.
The old man of the west

The man who says the law west of the Vlie sits by his fire at Medemelacha with a rug over his knees. He will not go in a boat again, but he will say it all three times, slowly, for whoever is to carry it.
A noble a hundred, a free man fifty, a half-free man twenty-five. Four, two, one. And men to swear with you by the same count. A child could keep it.
A wound we pay by its length. The others pay by what it did. Tell them that in the west a thumb's breadth is a thumb's breadth.
My daughter's son has all of it. He has sat at my knee nine winters.
I can say it backwards. I would like to see something that is not a cow.
If anyone asks you why it is so, say: because it was judged so. He will want a better reason. There is none better.
Learn it by heart, three times through
Take the grandson as a hand; he has it all
Cut the numbers on a tally stick

Three times through, and a fourth in the boat with the steersman hearing you. You have it: the numbers, the lengths, and which oath goes with which. The old man says you would have made a poor wise man and a good witness, and that the second is rarer.

The numbers stay. The lengths of wounds and their prices run together somewhere past the Vlie, and by Winaldum you have a hand's breadth costing what a hand costs. Wlemar hears you out and says the west will have to be content with its numbers.

The old man takes sixteen pennies for the boy's first summer and tells him to say the law every night before he sleeps, so that it does not wash out. The boy is aboard before the silver is counted. He rows badly and remembers everything.
A hundred, fifty, twenty-five: three rows of notches on a hazel stick. The old man looks at it for a while. That is what it costs, he says. It is not why. But a stick does not forget, and you might.
The emperor's question

Two of the emperor's messengers are at Dorestat, a count and a churchman, strangers to the district as the new order has it. The churchman's clerk is asking along the dam heads who knows the Frisians' law, and the toll man has pointed at you.

After harvest the emperor will have every people's law read before him at Aachen, mended where it needs it, and written. The Saxons' I have. The Franks' fills a chest. The Frisians' is not on any skin in the realm.
I am told it lives in two or three old men on mounds in the sea. I am told you know which mounds.
After this the judges judge by what is written, and take no gifts. That is the whole of it. You may tell your old men so.
The emperor pays carriage. Ten shillings of twelve, on the tally, to the man who brings them to the palace at Noviomagus. I pay for wise men delivered dry.
Undertake to bring the wise men to the palace
Tell the clerk what was said on the terp
Say you carry wool

The clerk counts a hundred and twenty pennies onto the toll man's table and splits a tally: your half, the emperor's half. The toll man watches silver go past him untaxed and breathes through his nose.

You tell him the three scales and what a shilling is in each. He writes fast and pays forty pennies for it. A week later a rider reaches Winaldum who already knows what a noble costs beyond the Lauwers, and Wlemar is not a man who wonders long how.

You say you carry wool. The clerk writes that down too. By midsummer a rider has found Winaldum without you, and Wlemar sends word that if he must go in a boat, he will go in one whose master he has seen swear.
Two wise men and one boat
The summons has come to Winaldum. Wlemar and Saxmund stand on the beach with a bundle each, and have been disagreeing since first light about what they will say when a Frank holds a pen over it.
We say all of it, as it was judged. A law is not what we would like to have judged.

All of it. Then say this to a bishop's clerk. Who breaks into a shrine and takes the holy things is led to the sand the tide covers. His ears are slit, he is gelded, and he is given to the gods he robbed. That is judged, beyond the Lauwers. I did not make it.
It is judged. Nobody has asked for it in my lifetime. The gods are owed a good deal they do not get.
And why should the emperor have our law in his chest while he keeps our sons off their fathers' land? Let him give that back. Then I will remember things for him.
The rider knew our numbers before he got down from his horse. Somebody reckons aloud.
You have heard both. You stand between Frisians and Franks every day and still have both ears. What would you say?
Say all of it, as it was judged
Say what a Christian king can put his name to
Ask for the land first
Wlemar says that makes two against one and gets into the boat as if the matter were closed. Saxmund gets in after him and says it is closed at Winaldum. It is a long way to Noviomagus.
Saxmund asks whether you sell short measure too. Wlemar says a merchant thinks of the buyer; it is his trade, not his fault. Both of them come aboard. Neither of them sits near you.

Saxmund looks at you for a while, as a man looks at a plank he had taken for rotten. Wlemar says a king gives nothing to a man who asks before he is asked, and then, more quietly, that it would need to be in writing, from somebody a palace believes.
Saint Martin's opinion
The way south goes up the Vecht under Saint Martin's. The bishop's deacon is waiting on the bank; news of two wise men in one boat has outrun you.

The bishop asks that some things be said first. That a man in feud has peace in church and on the way to it. And that work on the Lord's day is four shillings, twelve beyond the Lauwers, where they need it more.
And that one judgement be left where it lies. A book with the emperor's name on it cannot hand a man to devils on a beach.
I have a letter for the palace clerk that says so. It will get a Frisian through a door faster than his blood-price would.

If it is the widows of the Ems mouth your easterner is brooding on: that right was taken by law, for broken faith. What a law took, an emperor may give back. But it must be asked in writing, and Saint Martin's poor are many this year.
Take the bishop's letter to the palace clerk
Give alms for Saint Martin's poor, and ask him to write for the widow's sons
Say the wise men speak for themselves

The deacon reads the letter aloud to you once, pointing at the words, so that you know what you carry. You know four of the words by the end. Saxmund asks what it says. You tell him. He says the bishop has spared him the trouble of deciding what he thinks of bishops.

Twenty pennies go into the alms box. The deacon writes a second letter, shorter than the first: that the mother is baptised, that the sons were children in the year of the rising, and that the bishop of Saint Martin's asks mercy for them and those like them. He reads it to you, pointing. Saxmund hears it and looks at the river.

The deacon says the bishop will be sorry to hear it, in the voice of a man who will enjoy telling him. Wlemar says from the boat that he has peace in church by his own judgement and does not need a letter for it.
The palace above the Waal

Noviomagus is full of law. Saxons with the faces of hostages, Franks of the IJssel with a chest of their own, and clerks walking fast. The Frisians are to be heard after the Saxons, and the Saxons have a great deal to say.
Twelve days, if the Saxons are brief. They are not a brief people when it is about cattle.
I have waited sixty years for someone to ask. Twelve days will not hurt me. It may hurt your trade.
There is a doorkeeper here who can count to thirty. I watched him do it for a Saxon.
Two wise men, and dry. Your tally is good. I did not think to see it again.
Wait your turn behind the Saxons
Send in the bishop's letter
Find the doorkeeper who can count to thirty

Twelve days under the palace hill. Wlemar sits on the bank and tells the Saxons' law-men where their law and his agree, which is more often than either side likes. Your boat earns nothing. You learn what a Saxon noble costs, and it is a great deal.

The letter goes in by a boy and a clerk comes out by himself. Five days, he says, and the Frisians will be heard in the small room, where it is warmer. A bishop's seal is a kind of weather; doors open before it.
The doorkeeper counts to thirty without moving his lips. Three days, he says. Wlemar asks what you paid, and when you tell him he says that among Frisians it would have been a matter for the lots.
What is written

A bare room, a trestle, a clerk with a pen and a boy with a horn of ink. The wise men speak Frisian; the clerk has Frankish and Latin. You stand between, and what goes on the skin goes through your mouth.
Begin with what a man is worth. Everybody does.
Between the Vlie and the Lauwers: a noble, eighty shillings. Tell him. And tell him it is three pennies to the shilling, or he will think us rich.
Three scales? The emperor would like one. One is tidier.
And the west, as the old man gave it: four, two, one, and a wound by its length. Say it for him. You have it better than I do.
And the west: a hundred, fifty, twenty-five. The rest of the west stayed by a fire at Medemelacha. Tell him the numbers.
Now the sand. Say it to him as I say it. I want to watch his pen.
My hand is cold, the ink is thin, and now there are gods in it.
Or say nothing more yet. He has asked us for a great deal. Nobody in this room has asked him for anything.
Put it into Frankish as they say it, all of it
Help the clerk make one clean law of it
Lay the letter for the widow's sons on the trestle before a word is said
Tell them it has kept in their heads this long

You put it across as it comes: three scales, the lots on the altar, the kettle, the Lord's day, the harper's hand, the river that may not be blocked, and the sand the tide covers. The clerk writes all of it. At the head of two leaves he writes whose judgements they are: Wlemar's, and Saxmund's. Then he sands the last leaf and says it will want tidying, later.

You and the clerk make one law of it. One scale, in the emperor's pennies. The church's peace first. The lots stay, since they lie on an altar. The sand goes: you simply do not put it into Frankish. Saxmund understands more Frankish than he has let on. He does not speak to you again on that side of the Lauwers.

You lay the bishop's letter on the trestle before the first word. The clerk reads it twice and takes it out of the room. He is gone until the lamps are lit. When he comes back he says the emperor will hear the Frisians' law, and after it the matter of the sons of those who rose. Saxmund sits down. It is the first time you have seen him do it. Then the wise men say their law, all of it, and the clerk writes.

You turn to the wise men and say it in Frisian: it has kept in your heads this long. Wlemar looks at the pen, and at Saxmund, and says he is outvoted by a merchant. He gets up. The clerk asks what was said. You tell him the Frisians find they have forgotten their law, and will send word if it comes back to them.
As it was said
Winaldum, after the assembly. Wlemar is back on his mound. The clerk's leaves went to Aachen in a chest with the Saxons' law and the rest, and were read out before the emperor, the old gods and all.
They read it out. The emperor asked whether the sand was still used. The clerk said he would ask. Nobody has asked.
It was to be mended and written fair. I think they have a great many laws to mend, and one clerk with cold hands. It will lie as it is. I have seen worse things happen to a law.
The three lands gave a penny a hearth for the man who carried it. It comes to more than I thought. There are more hearths than I knew.
And this, which is not silver. In any court from the Zwin to the Weser, when you swear, your oath is taken as a man's of that land. You will not go looking for helpers at dusk again.
He wrote our names over it. Mine and Saxmund's. I had not thought to be written. I find I do not mind as much as I should.
Take the hearth pennies and the oath-right
Take less silver, and his sister's son to keep your goods here
Ask for a house plot by the landing as well

Eight hundred pennies in three bags, one from each land, and the eastern bag the lightest and the most carefully tied. Wlemar says your name at the next court day, and what it is now worth. The law lies in a chest at Aachen as it was said, and nobody mends it.

Six hundred pennies, and a young man of Wlemar's kin who can count and has been told what happens to a man who counts wrong for a friend of the three lands. Your goods will lie dry on the terp. The law lies in a chest at Aachen as it was said, and nobody mends it.

Wlemar walks you to the foot of the terp and paces out a strip between the landing and the sheep track. Nobody carried it truer, he says, the west and all. Nine hundred pennies, a kinsman to keep your goods, and ground of your own among the Frisians of the middle land. The law lies in a chest at Aachen as it was said.
The emperor's law of the Frisians
Dorestat, after the assembly. The clerk is back from Aachen with a fair copy under his arm and a sealed skin for you. The toll man is reading the seal upside down and not liking it.
It was read before the emperor from the first word to the last, and he did not stop it once. He stopped the Saxons' four times.
One scale. The church's peace at the head. No gods anywhere. It is to be read out at every court from the Zwin to the Weser, and the judges are to judge by it.
This is yours. The emperor's own word that your boat pays no toll at Dorestat, in his time and his son's.
I knew a man who had one of those. He was an abbot.
I am told the old men beyond the Lauwers do not thank you. Old men do not thank pens. Their grandsons will not know there was ever another way.
Take the charter and the emperor's silver
Take the charter; send the silver to the widow at the Ems mouth
Ask to be reckoned among the emperor's own merchants

Nine hundred pennies and a skin with the emperor's seal. The toll man waves you past with two fingers. East of the Lauwers a law is read out at the courts that no one there remembers judging, and at the Ems mouth they know which boat carried it to the pen.

You keep two hundred pennies and the charter, and send the rest east with a man you trust, for the widow and for those like her. Word comes back in spring: Saxmund has said at a court day that the merchant is a fool about laws and not about people. From him it is a good deal.

The clerk says the numbers in the fair copy were right the first time, which he has not seen before, and writes your name on a second skin: a merchant under the palace's own protection, answerable to the emperor's court and no other. Eleven hundred pennies. East of the Lauwers they know which boat carried the law to the pen.
The sons of ninety-three

The Ems mouth, after the assembly. The count's man has ridden off the widow's farm with his tally sticks, and there is smoke from more roofs than there was. Saxmund is waiting at the landing, which he has not done before.

It was given at Aachen, after the law was read. The sons of those who rose have their fathers' land again, Frisians and Saxons both. The emperor said it was mercy. The clerk wrote it as law, which is better. Mercy dies with the man.
My eldest ploughed the long field yesterday. It is the same field. He ploughed it as if it were another.
And our law is written, sand and all. I said every word. I find a man remembers better when he has been paid first.
Every house that has its land again has sent something down for you. Some sent silver. Most sent what they had: cloth, hides. Do not weigh it in front of them.
There is ground by the landing that is nobody's. It is yours. Ask for something else as well. I am not often in this temper.
Take the ground by the landing and what the houses sent
Ask for the younger son to keep your goods here
Ask for the elder son as a sworn partner, with a boat of his own

A strip of ground above the tide mark, five hundred pennies in small silver, eight bolts of good grey cloth and ten hides. You do not weigh any of it in front of them. East of the Lauwers, fathers leave land to sons again, twelve years before anyone had a right to hope for it.

The younger son is seventeen and has never been further than Leer. He will keep your goods on your own ground by the landing and send word by any boat going west. His mother tells him, in front of you, what she will do if he counts short. East of the Lauwers, fathers leave land to sons again.

Saxmund is silent a while, and then says the boy has a field now and may not want a boat. The boy says he wants both. They swear it at the landing, his hand and yours on the same oar: one purse, two boats, and the truth told between them. East of the Lauwers, fathers leave land to sons again.
Kept in the head
Doccinga, after the assembly. The two wise men are in Boniface's church, by the altar where the twigs lay. The emperor's chest went to Aachen with a gap in it the size of the Frisians.
The emperor was told the Frisians are a forgetful people. They say he laughed. With an emperor that is not always good.
So it is still ours. A count who wants to know the law here must ask a Frisian, and wait for the answer.
And when I die it is a little smaller, unless I have said it to somebody. That is the price. I had hoped a skin would pay it for me.
We have put our hands on this altar for you. In the three lands you have peace in your boat, at the landing and on the way to both, as a man has in his own house. Who breaks it pays ninefold.
The clerk will remember your face. Sell elsewhere than Noviomagus for a year or two.
Take the peace of the three lands and the hearth pennies
Ask as well for a man who knows the Lauwers mouth
Ask to be taught the law itself, all three lands

Seven hundred pennies, a penny a hearth from three lands, and a peace that every Frisian court will hold to. The law goes home in two grey heads. Nothing of it is on any skin in the realm, and the palace knows whose boat that was.

Six hundred pennies and the peace, and a fisherman of Saxmund's kin who takes you out on the ebb and shows you the Lauwers mouth: where the channel runs this year, and the three ways to tell when it has moved. Nothing of the law is on any skin in the realm, and the palace knows whose boat that was.

It takes most of a winter by Wlemar's fire: the middle land from him, the east from Saxmund, the west from your own mouth while both of them mend it. At the end Wlemar says you are to say it to your heir, whole, before you are too old to be corrected. Nine hundred pennies and the peace besides. The law is in three heads now, and one of them sails.
What the son gave back
The Ems mouth, a long time after. A man of thirty is setting boundary stakes along a ditch as if each one were a nail in something. He knows your boat before he knows you.

The old emperor died at Aachen in the winter. His son has given back what the father took: the right of the fathers' land, to Saxons and Frisians both. Some say he is generous. The count's man says he is a fool.
My mother did not see it. She ground her corn on your kind of stone until the stone was a plate, and said every day that a king's anger does not last as long as a ditch.
My uncle Saxmund says it should not have needed a king's death. He says most things should not have needed what they needed.
They read us the emperor's law every court day. There was nothing in it about us. It took a new king to find the room.
He says also that your house asked for this before anyone was listening. We do not forget that here. We do not forget anything here; it is all we own.
It was your father's boat, then. You have his way of looking at a landing.
Be remembered as the house that asked first
Ask what a farm with an heir needs
Wish him a dry harvest and go

He sends a boy running. By evening there are two hundred pennies on your thwart from houses you have never traded with, an order for iron, and a cousin of his who will keep your goods at the landing and count them twice. Twelve years is not long, east of the Lauwers.

Iron, he says. Spades, a plough share, nails. A man does not mend what may be taken from his sons, and nothing here has been mended for twenty years. Every farm from here to the Weser will say the same this spring.
He thanks you and drives in another stake. There are a great many still to do.

The Frisians' law has been written for the emperor, as two old men of the terps said it: three lands, three prices for a man, and an old judgement about the tide sand that the clerk wrote down with the rest.
The emperor has given the Frisians one written law, read out at every court from the Zwin to the Weser. The judges are to judge by the writing and take no gifts.
At Aachen the emperor has given back to the Frisians and Saxons who rose the right to leave land to their sons. Beyond the Lauwers the count's men are riding off the farms.
The emperor asked for the Frisians' law and was told they had forgotten it. The Saxons' law fills a book. The Frisians' is where it was, in the heads of old men on mounds.

Inside a small timber church at Doccinga, grey morning light from the door: a boy of eight reaches for two twigs wrapped in white wool on a plain altar, a priest and a grey-bearded lawman watching, seven men in wool cloaks standing in a row behind, one of them a boatman with tarred hands.

A sod-walled farmhouse on a low terp at the Ems mouth, flat grey tide flats behind, late afternoon: a lean man of forty-five sits mending a net and does not look up, a widow in a dark head-cloth stands in the doorway with a worn quernstone at her feet, the merchant before them with his cap in his hand.

The top of the terp at Winaldum on a windy bright day, sheep and the sea behind: two men sit on a turf bench with three heaps of beans on a cloak between them, the older counting on his fingers, the younger with folded arms, the merchant kneeling with a handful of silver pennies.

Inside a low house at Medemelacha by firelight: a very old man with a rug over his knees holds up four, then two, then one finger, a boy of seventeen crouched at his knee mouthing the words, the merchant on a stool with a hazel stick and a knife, a cow's head showing over the byre wall.

A dam head at Dorestat on a spring morning, boats and casks along the bank: a young tonsured clerk with wax tablets faces the merchant, a Frankish count in a red cloak stands behind with a hand on his sword belt, and the toll man at his table points at the merchant with his tally stick.

The beach below the terp at Winaldum at first light, the small boat drawn up with her mast stepped: two lawmen with a bundle each stand arguing, the older calm with his hand raised, the younger pointing out at the wet sand the tide has left, the crew waiting at the oars.

The bank of the Vecht at Traiectum under a stone church and the old fort wall, a still overcast noon: a deacon in a white alb holds out a folded, sealed letter over the gunwale, two Frisian lawmen sitting in the boat with their backs half turned, the merchant standing between.

The river bank below the palace hill at Noviomagus, timber halls and a stone chapel above, afternoon sun: groups of Saxons and Franks wait with chests and bundles, clerks hurry between them, and two Frisian lawmen sit on the merchant's upturned boat watching a doorkeeper count coins.

A bare whitewashed room in the palace, one small window, lamp not yet lit: a clerk at a trestle with a pen raised over a skin, a boy holding an ink horn, two Frisian lawmen standing opposite, and the merchant between the two sides with one hand toward each.

The terp at Winaldum in late autumn, low sun and long shadows: the old lawman paces out a strip of ground between the landing and a sheep track, three tied bags of silver on the turf bench behind him, the merchant's boat on the beach below.

The toll table at Dorestat on a cold clear morning: the clerk, back from Aachen in a travelling cloak, hands the merchant a skin with a hanging wax seal, a bound book under his other arm, the toll man leaning over to read the seal upside down with his mouth turned down.

The landing at the Ems mouth in autumn, smoke rising from a dozen low roofs on the terp behind: the lean lawman stands waiting at the water's edge, the widow beside him with two grown sons, and on the sand a heap of folded grey cloth, hides and a small bag, a rider going away small across the marsh.

Inside the timber church at Doccinga, evening, one candle: the two lawmen stand with their right hands flat on the altar and look at the merchant, the old one tired, the younger almost smiling; the altar is bare where a book might lie.

A field edge at the Ems mouth in spring twelve years on, wide sky and wet ditches: a man of thirty in a patched tunic drives a boundary stake with a wooden maul, a line of fresh stakes behind him, a worn-out quernstone set as a step at the house door, the merchant's boat in the creek.
